Re-elect · SMUHSD School Board, Trustee Area 3
# I know this district — because I've been showing up for it.
Four years of institutional knowledge, working relationships, and daily presence at school sites across San Mateo Union High School District, where I currently serve as Board Vice President. There's unfinished work worth finishing, and if re-elected, I'm ready to serve as Board President.
Proven. Prepared. Present.
Get Involved Hear From Teachers
► Watch the video · 0:30
Watch the video 0:30
Watch the video 1:00
Phone-free school days
## I fought for phone-free schools. Now teachers say it's working.
I was the only trustee on the working group that wrote our phone-free policy, and I pushed for it to cover the whole school day. Two months in, here's what teachers and principals told the board:
- ✓Students are talking to each other againGreeting one another and talking with their teachers as they walk into class.
- ✓More focused and engaged in classPresent, and more willing to take a chance on a question or an idea.
- ✓Suspensions cut in halfReported by the assistant principal at Mills High.
"I can't imagine going to school a different way."Assistant Principal, Hillsdale High School
Share this video See all videos
Track record
## Four years of work, at a glance
Nine things I personally identified and pushed to get done — not just votes I cast. Tap any one for the full story.
✓ Expanded college-level dual enrollment courses. ✓ Built career pathways in construction, business, and healthcare. ✓ Opened new graduation pathways for Special Ed students. ✓ Made every school phone-free. ✓ Drove responsible AI guidance. ✓ Expanded wraparound support for at-promise students. ✓ Launched twice-yearly reading & math assessments. ✓ Pushed for more support for multilingual learners and their teachers. ✓ Created a PE study hall for student-athletes.
See the full track record →

Platform for the next term
## Continuing the work, not starting over
Three priorities, each building directly on something already underway.
🎓
### College & Career Readiness
Expanding access to advanced coursework and CTE pathways — and turning assessment data into action for every student.
Read more → 🛡️
### Safe & Connected Schools
Helping students navigate pressure and build real connection — through a phone-free school day, responsible AI use, a school culture that welcomes open, respectful discussion, and a firm commitment that every student, no matter their background or identity, feels safe, respected, and supported.
Read more → 🧭
### Fiscal Responsibility
Planning ahead responsibly — leading our next Five-Year Strategic Plan and investing wisely in the facilities and programs that serve students first.
Read more →
Read the full platform →

Why I'm running again
## The work isn't finished — and I'm the one who started it.
Knowledge
#### A steep learning curve, already climbed
Governance takes years to understand fully. Many of my priorities are multi-year initiatives I want to see through, not hand off mid-stream.
Relationships
#### Working relationships that get things done
Strong, established relationships with the Superintendent, fellow trustees, and district staff — the kind that make real progress possible.
Investment
#### Still personally invested
Two of my five children have graduated from SMUHSD and I have three more to go. I'm invested in great schools for all.
Presence
#### Time to actually show up
Site visits, board meetings, professional development, task forces — the job takes time and presence, not just good intentions. I have both.
Trustee Area 3
## What's happening close to home
Area 3 covers Aragon and Hillsdale High Schools and the neighborhoods around them — Hillsborough, the San Mateo Highlands, and West San Mateo. San Mateo High, right next door, is part of the same community many Area 3 families are part of. And because Hillsborough addresses split across attendance zones, many Area 3 families have students at Burlingame High too — not just Aragon and Hillsdale.
Aragon and Hillsdale are where a lot of my track record started — including the PE study hall fix, which began with my own daughter at Hillsdale, and the Peace Pantry, which I still volunteer at weekly. Here's what's new at the site level this year:
- ● San Mateo High opened a new 20,000-sq-ft athletic training complex this year, funded by the Measure L bond
- ● Burlingame High opened a brand-new gym this year for its students and families — also funded by Measure L
- ● A new hands-on trades program at Aragon — the only one of its kind in the county
- ● Two new Pacific Islander mentoring groups at Aragon through Empower San Mateo
- ● New career pathway courses launching at both Hillsdale and Aragon
- ● A reordered math sequence at Hillsdale, now showing real results in Algebra 2
See what's happening site-by-site →
Mother of five — all raised and educated in San Mateo public schools.
About
## A present, engaged parent-neighbor — not a career politician
I'm the mother of five children, all raised and educated in San Mateo public schools. I joined the Board four years ago because none of the sitting trustees had children currently enrolled in our schools — a genuine parent's perspective was missing from the table. My two daughters have since graduated from Hillsdale High School during my time on the Board, and my three sons will follow.
I hold an M.S. in Nutritional Science from BYU and am a Registered Dietitian, though I paused that career to raise my family. My science background is why I look for evidence-based practice and data-driven decisions. I've also run a portrait photography business serving local families for 17 years — work that's kept me closely connected to families across our community and given me a front-row seat to what our kids are really going through. I'm also active in interfaith community service through the Peninsula Multifaith Coalition, work that reflects the same value I try to bring to the Board: finding common ground and getting things done for kids, across our differences.
Right now, I'm honored to serve as Board Vice President, and I'd be ready to serve as President if re-elected. My flexible work schedule means I can actually show up — school site visits, professional development, and district events during the school day. This job requires time and presence, not just good intentions, and I bring both. I also show up outside board meetings, at school sports and performances, and volunteering weekly at Empower San Mateo's Peace Pantry with my own kids.

The full story
# Every priority, in detail
The homepage covers the headlines. Here's the fuller story behind each one — what the problem was, what I did, and what's next — plus the full platform and a closer look at Area 3.
Track Record Platform Area 3 District Results →
Track record
## Problems I spotted. Work I drove. Momentum I'm continuing.
These are initiatives I personally identified and pushed forward — not just votes I cast.
College & career
### Growing Access to College-Level Courses
Dual enrollment lets students take real community college classes while still in high school — both high school and college credit, at no cost to families.
"Every student who wants to stretch academically should have a real path to do it — not just the students who were already headed to a four-year school."
DidSupported the growth of dual-enrollment partnerships with Skyline College, Cañada College, and College of San Mateo — now offering 60+ dual-enrollment opportunities across all six comprehensive high schools, with students passing at a 93–99% rate. Helped secure CAPP grant funding, including $100,000 at San Mateo High alone, to fund counselor time and add more sections. NextAddress the broader dip in students accessing two or more college-level courses (AP, dual enrollment, or IB) by senior year — down 11 points districtwide this past year. That's a centerpiece of my College & Career Readiness priority for next term.
Learn more
Dual-enrollment access has grown across subjects like Administration of Justice, Architecture and Engineering, Digital Media, Business, Psychology, Kinesiology, Interior Design, and Early Childhood Education.
At the same time, the district's own data shows the share of students accessing at least two college-level courses by senior year fell from 63.4% to 52.1% this past year — a real dip I'm not going to paper over. Growing dual enrollment is part of the answer; so is revisiting graduation requirements so students have room in their schedule for rigor, not just CTE.
College & career
### Building Career Pathways in Construction, Business, and Healthcare
A recent county Grand Jury report found career-pathway completion averages just 15% countywide — and our numbers echo that. Most students try one career class, but few finish a full sequence that actually prepares them for a job or a trade.
"Trying one class isn't the same as finishing a pathway. I want every student who starts one to be able to finish it."
DidPushed the district to act on the Grand Jury's findings: helped create a CTE Coordinator role, start new pathways in Healthcare and Business & Entrepreneurship, and supported approval of the new hands-on construction and trades program at Aragon High — the only one of its kind in the county. NextThese pathways just launched, so I want to see real completion data in my next term. I'm also pushing for students to go deeper in one area instead of sampling all three, so they have room in their schedule to finish what they start.
Learn more
"CTE" stands for Career Technical Education — hands-on classes in fields like healthcare, business, and the trades. A student "completes a pathway" by finishing a sequence of 2–3 connected courses in one field, not just trying a single class.
Since I began raising this, the district has stood up a CTE Coordinator role, approved new course outlines, and launched new pathways using Golden State Pathways and Strong Workforce grant funding — at no new cost to local taxpayers. Nearly all students (95%) now take at least one CTE course; the next challenge is pathway completion, where only about 5–10% of students finish a full sequence. I'm also continuing to press on the pay gap that makes it hard to hire CTE teachers with real industry experience.
What people are saying
Student support
### New Graduation Pathways for Special Education Students
For years, students with the most significant support needs had very few real options for earning a diploma. The Board adopted new pathways to change that.
"A diploma should be within real reach for every student, including students with the most significant support needs — not just on paper."
DidSupported the Board's approval of an Inclusive Diploma pathway for students with significant cognitive disabilities, and a reduced-credit pathway (175 credits) for students with disabilities whose IEP team determines it's the right fit. Result24 students are projected to graduate this year through the new pathway — up from just 5 the year before.
Learn more
Before these changes, students with the most significant cognitive disabilities had no real pathway to a diploma, and many students with IEPs were on track to age out without one. The state convened a workgroup to address dismal postsecondary outcomes for these students and opened the door to an Inclusive Diploma option; our Board paired that with a reduced-credit pathway so an IEP team can determine, student by student, whether it's the right fit.
My priority now is making sure every eligible family actually knows this option exists.
Phones & wellness
### A Phone-Free School Day, Built With the Community
When a new state law required schools to set a phone policy, I was the only trustee who joined the district's working group — students, parents, teachers, and staff — to help build it from scratch.
"We need to give our kids back their lives — detach from screens and have real, tactile experiences."
DidPushed for a policy covering the whole school day, not just class time. It passed 5–0. NextMaking sure it's implemented well this fall, alongside a promised digital-wellness curriculum that teaches kids healthy tech habits, not just a rule to follow.
Learn more
The Board studied this for months, including surveys of teachers, parents, and more than 4,000 students, before voting unanimously in March 2026 for a "bell-to-bell" policy — no phones for the entire school day, not just during class. San Mateo High has run a similar policy successfully for years, which helped inform the districtwide approach.
What people are saying
Future-ready
### Getting Ahead of AI
Rather than ignore how students already use AI, I asked the Superintendent to make districtwide AI policy a formal goal — and I was the only trustee to join the district's AI Task Force of students, teachers, parents, and staff.
"AI isn't going away. I made sure our schools got ahead of it instead of scrambling to catch up."
DidThe task force met through spring 2026 and presented a balanced plan on teaching, privacy, and honest use at a public meeting. NextTurning that plan into real classroom training for teachers and clear guidance for families this fall.
Learn more
The task force wrestled with a hard question: what should AI never replace? Everyone agreed it should never replace real relationships between teachers and students. My focus has been on the incentive problem — if a tool gets a student a better grade with less effort, how do we make sure they're still learning something, not just shortcutting the work?
What people are saying
At-promise students
### Empower San Mateo
It started small: Empowerment Through Action (ETA), a mentoring and support program at Hillsdale High for kids facing poverty, housing instability, and hunger. It worked so well we're now bringing that model to more schools as Empower San Mateo — and I show up for it personally.
"I don't just vote for this program — I show up on Friday mornings to hand out food at the Peace Pantry with my own kids."
DidVolunteered weekly at the Peace Pantry; championed the grant funding that helped ETA's model expand beyond Hillsdale. NextSupporting careful, well-funded expansion to more school sites as partnerships mature — not growing faster than we can support well.
Learn more
ETA launched at Hillsdale High in 2018 and now supports more than 200 students there with tutoring, mentoring, family support, and the Peace Pantry, which feeds about 140 families a week. In June 2025, the Board voted to expand that model — as Empower San Mateo — to San Mateo High, Aragon High, Bridge Academy, and Abbott Middle School, backed by nearly $1 million in state grant funding and about $500,000 in nonprofit support over two years. Rollout began in early 2026 and continues through the next several years, including new middle school partnerships.
Two new Pacific Islander mentoring groups launched at Aragon this school year as part of that expansion — more in the Area 3 section below.
What people are saying
Data that acts
### Twice-Yearly Reading & Math Assessments
When I joined the Board, the only common measure of academic skills we had was a single 11th-grade state exam that didn't count toward a grade, was given once a year, and told us almost nothing about how an individual student was actually doing from month to month or grade to grade.
"One test in four years told us almost nothing. Now we can catch a struggling student before they fall behind, not after."
DidPushed for a consistent assessment system that tracks student growth in reading and math across every grade and every school, all year long — not just one snapshot at the end of high school. NextMaking sure that data actually drives immediate teaching adjustments and targeted help for students who are falling behind — not just sitting in a report nobody reads until the following year.
Learn more
The district now runs MAP assessments in reading and math twice a year at every school, giving teachers and counselors a real, ongoing picture of how each student is progressing — instead of one snapshot at the end of 11th grade.
Teachers and counselors now review this data together several times a year to flag students who need extra support early, rather than waiting for a single end-of-year test to tell us who struggled. My next priority is making sure every school follows through with fast, consistent intervention whenever the data shows a student is falling behind.
Multilingual learners
### Fixing a Broken Rule for Multilingual Learners
A state review found the district had kept Multilingual Learners — students still learning English — in separate classes longer than state law allows. The district's fix then swung too far the other way, moving students into standard classes too fast, before some teachers had the training to support them.
"I listened to teachers, compared our policy to what the law actually requires, and fixed a rule that was hurting both students and staff."
DidDuring a professional development day I attended in person, I talked directly with teachers about what wasn't working, then compared our policy line-by-line against the actual legal requirements, drafted a fix, and had it reviewed by legal counsel before bringing it to the Board. ResultPassed unanimously, paired with new training for standard-class teachers who now receive Multilingual Learners. Outcomes for these students have improved since — and the Board has since approved a companion graduation pathway so Multilingual Learners who need it can focus on core content and language proficiency toward a diploma.
Learn more
A routine state compliance audit found SMUHSD had kept Multilingual Learners in separate designated classes longer than state law allows. In response, the district moved students into standard classes very quickly — sometimes before they were ready, and before their new teachers had the training to support them well.
I only found out how this was playing out because I was in the room at a teacher professional development day — one of the advantages of having the flexibility to actually show up during the school day. I followed up with more conversations afterward, checked our policy against the real Education Code requirements myself, and worked with legal counsel to get it right before bringing a fix to the Board.
Student wellness
### A Study Hall Option for Student-Athletes
Before I joined the Board, every student had to take PE in 9th and 10th grade — no exceptions, even for kids already training hard in a school sport, dance, or marching band. I watched student-athletes and performers run on empty: overscheduled, overtraining, injured, and up past midnight on homework after a long practice.
"Kids were getting hurt from too much activity, not too little. I found a solution to fix that without cutting a single class."
DidWorked directly with our Superintendent and PE teachers to design a fix that didn't break any state rules or cost a PE teacher their job — and the Board approved it. Result10th graders playing a school-sponsored sport can now take a study hall period instead of PE during their season, giving them back the time and rest they need to stay healthy and keep their grades up.
Learn more
Before this change, PE was mandatory in 9th and 10th grade with no exceptions, even for students already logging hours of physical activity through school sports or dance. Some student-athletes were getting hurt from doing too much, not too little, and losing study time they needed to keep their grades up.
I raised this directly with our Superintendent and PE staff and helped design a fix: 10th graders playing a school-sponsored sport can take a study hall period in place of PE during their season, without cutting a single PE section or breaking state education code.
Platform for the next term
## Continuing the work, not starting over
Every priority below builds directly on something already underway — this is unfinished, multi-year work I'm positioned to see through.
🎓
### College & Career Readiness
CTE
#### From CTE access to CTE completion — and stronger academic rigor
I will explore a pathway-style graduation requirement — letting students go deeper in career training, arts, or world language rather than sampling all three — so more students can finish a full pathway, not just start one. Any change would need real input from teachers and staff first. I also want to address the recent dip in A-G completion and access to college-level coursework for students who want it.
📊
#### From data collection to data action
I want to move us beyond simply gathering assessment data toward districtwide practices that turn it into fast, targeted instruction and intervention.
🛡️
### Safe & Connected Schools
📵
#### Phone-free policy done right
I will make sure implementation goes well this fall, and that we follow through on the promised digital citizenship and wellness curriculum.
AI
#### AI in the classroom, from policy to practice
Progress from task force recommendations to established classroom practice, with teacher training and clear communication with families.
💬
#### Building a culture of civil discourse
District survey data shows only 32% of students feel comfortable expressing views on controversial topics in class, and 67% feel they can't share an opinion for fear of how it will be received. I want to build a district culture of robust, respectful discourse and free expression — essential for raising independent thinkers and engaged citizens.
🏳️‍⚧️
#### Every student safe, respected, and supported
In September 2025, the Board voted unanimously to strengthen nondiscrimination protections for transgender and gender-nonconforming students — covering respect for a student's gender identity, use of names and pronouns, equal access to school facilities and activities, and dress code freedom consistent with gender identity.
"I support our transgender students. Period. I've listened to transgender students and their families, and those conversations have deepened my understanding of what it means for every student to feel safe, respected, and supported at school. I am committed to ensuring our district is a place where every student is treated with dignity and has the opportunity to thrive."
🛡️
One throughline: building connection in a fast-changing world A phone-free school day, responsible AI use, and a stronger culture of honest, respectful dialogue aren't separate issues — all are about giving students the tools to build real connection, protect essential learning, communicate openly, and be prepared for a fast-changing world. This is also the thinking behind a meeting I helped convene between the Superintendent and the Pacific Islander community — bringing people together across difference, a model I want to build on districtwide.
🧭
### Fiscal Responsibility
🏗️
#### Investing in growth that serves students first
From Aragon's long-requested stadium expansion to the new, purpose-built Bridge Academy campus now in design, I want to make sure facility growth is planned around real student needs as part of this fall's Facilities Master Plan.
5YR
#### Leading the district's next Five-Year Strategic Plan
The Superintendent has signaled it's time to begin a new five-year plan. I want to lead that work — asking hard questions, digging into Ed Code and dense policy language, and helping the Board prioritize resources around what actually serves students.
🤝
#### Scaling Empower San Mateo sustainably
I want to support careful, well-resourced expansion to more school sites as funding and partnerships mature — not growth for its own sake.
Trustee Area 3
## What's happening close to home
Area 3 covers Aragon and Hillsdale High Schools and the neighborhoods around them — Hillsborough, the San Mateo Highlands, and West San Mateo. San Mateo High, right next door, is part of the same community many Area 3 families are part of. A few things happening at our local schools this year.
Aragon and Hillsdale are the two comprehensive high schools serving this part of the district, and they're where a lot of my track record started — including the PE study hall fix, which began with my own daughter at Hillsdale, and the Peace Pantry, which I still volunteer at weekly.
Trustee area lines and school attendance lines aren't the same thing, though — Hillsborough addresses split across attendance zones, so a good number of Area 3 families have students at Burlingame High as well, not just Aragon and Hillsdale.
Here's what's new at the site level this year.
#### A New Turf Softball Field for Aragon
At our last board meeting, we approved the design for a new synthetic turf softball field at Aragon — new dugouts and other upgrades to match the investment our baseball field got last year. Between design and the state's required review process, the field is expected to be playable by early 2028. Our softball program deserves the same level of support.
#### Keys to Building a Tech Healthy Household
On September 16, I helped bring a parent workshop to the district — "Keys to Building a Tech Healthy Household," presented in partnership with Project Reboot — timed early in the school year alongside the rollout of our new phone-free school policy. Parents left with practical tools: a parent handbook, a dinner-table discussion guide, and more.
#### A New Athletic Training Complex at San Mateo High
San Mateo High opened a new 20,000-square-foot athletic complex this year — a gym, team and training rooms, a classroom, and seating for 820 spectators — funded by the Measure L bond voters approved in 2020. It's part of the same wave of facility investment that's already reached Aragon and Hillsdale.
#### A Brand-New Gym at Burlingame High
Burlingame High opened a brand-new gymnasium this year — a full-size gym, weight room, locker rooms, and practice space — funded by the Measure L bond voters approved in 2020. A meaningful number of Area 3 families have students at Burlingame High, and it's seen the same level of facility investment as Aragon, Hillsdale, and San Mateo High.
#### A New Trade Training Program at Aragon
Aragon launched a hands-on trades program this year — the only one of its kind at a San Mateo County high school. Students learn construction math, safety, and job-site skills, and can earn a real safety certification before they even graduate. It's for students who want a skilled trade, not just a four-year degree.
What people are saying
#### New Pacific Islander Mentoring Groups
As Empower San Mateo expanded to Aragon this year, two new Pacific Islander mentoring groups launched with weekly meetings — giving those students a consistent, supportive space at school. It's a direct outgrowth of the community relationship-building I've done, including helping convene a meeting between the Superintendent and the Pacific Islander community.
#### New Career Pathway Courses at Hillsdale and Aragon
Both of our Area 3 high schools are deepening career training this year. Aragon piloted a new Business & Entrepreneurship pathway that's now expanding to Hillsdale, and Aragon has also added a new Interior Design pathway — part of the district's broader push to help students go deeper in one field instead of just sampling a single class.
#### A Smarter Math Sequence at Hillsdale
Hillsdale reordered its standard math sequence — Geometry in 9th grade, Algebra in 10th. After 3 years of tracking, the results are in: more students are now succeeding in Algebra 2 as a result. It's the kind of site-level instructional change I want to see studied and, where it works, considered for other schools.
#### Stadium Seating at Aragon
Aragon's new turf baseball and flex field opened last spring — a great win for our athletes. But the stadium next door still seats only about 650 for a student body of 1,680, the tightest capacity in the district, and families have been asking for more room for six years. I'll give this need the consideration it deserves when we look at this fall's Facilities Master Plan.
